9. There is presumption of abandoned character of the property if it attracts the definition of abandoned property and the onus to rebut the presumption in the person who claims otherwise, that is to say, the property is not an abandoned property. So also, the publication of the lists shall have legal presumption that the buildings have been legally enlisted as abandoned property and vested in the Government. After the publication of the lists, any person interested in the said property claiming any right or interest in any of the buildings, which is included in any lists before a court or settlement constituted in exercise of powers under section 9 of the Ordinance is required to prove that the building is not an abandoned property and has not been vested in the Government under PO.16 of 1972. The onus squarely lies on the person who claims the exclusion of the building from the lists. This presumption is closely allied to the subject of burden proof under the Evidence Act. When the burden of proof of a fact is on a party, it may be said that there is presumption as to non-existence of that fact, and where there is a presumption as to existence of a fact, the burden of proving the non-existence of that fact is on the party who asserts its non-existence. These are established principles of presumption of fact. 

 10. A presumption is a rule of law that the courts shall draw a particular inference from a particular fact, unless and until the truth of such inference is disproved by the person who asserts its non-existence. A presumption of law is a rule of law that a particular inference shall be drawn by a court from a particular circumstance. Some of these presumptions are natural presumptions which the law simply recognizes and enforce. There presumptions of law are, however, rebuttable and these presumptions are intendments made by law, but, unlike them, they only hold good until disproved. In presumptions of law, the law peremptorily requires a certain inference to the made whenever the facts appear which it assumes as the basis of that inference. As presumptions of law are, in reality, rules of law, and part of the law itself, the court may draw inference whenever the requisite facts are before it. In case of presumption of law, the law declares a certain inference to be made whenever facts appear which it assumes on the basis of that inference. It is to be borne in mind that it is the established principles of law that the presumption is always in favour of the constitutionality of an enactment the reason is obvious. It is assumed that the legislature understands and correctly appreciates the needs of its own people that its laws are directed to problems made manifests by experience and its determinations are based on adequate grounds. It is presumed that the legislature does not make mistakes or omissions. In the words of lord Halsbury, A court of law is bound to proceed on the assumption that the legislature is an ideal person that does not make mistakes (Pemsel, 1891 AC 531 (549). 

 19. In Hazerullah V. Chairman, 1st Court, 3 BLC (AD) 42, a question arose about the legality of the enlistment of the property as the Government was not in possession of the property but the property was enlisted under section 5(1) (a) of the Ordinance. A five member Bench of this Division held that 'This contention will stand only when the claimant can prove that the disputed building was not an abandoned property.' Similar view was taken in Government of Bangladesh V. K.M. Zaker Hossain, 23 BLD (AD) 24. The principle is that if the property has declared as abandoned property and a Gazette notification has been passed, there is presumption that it has been legally declared as abandoned property and in such cases the enlistment of the building either in (a) or (b) list or that proper service of notice is immaterial unless the claimant can prove that the property is not abandoned property.
